question: The four osteopathic tenets begin: the body is a __________.
cited_learning_objective: State the first osteopathic tenet.
answer: unit
rationale: The first tenet is that the body is a unit.
accept: unit of body, mind, and spirit

question: The four osteopathic tenets include: the body is __________ and __________.
cited_learning_objective: State the self-regulation tenet.
answer: self-regulating, self-healing
rationale: The body is self-regulating and self-healing.

question: The four osteopathic tenets include: __________ and __________ are reciprocally related.
cited_learning_objective: State the structure-function tenet.
answer: structure, function
rationale: Structure and function are reciprocally related.

question: The four osteopathic tenets close with: __________ treatment is based on applying these principles.
cited_learning_objective: State the rational-treatment tenet.
answer: rational
rationale: Rational treatment is based on applying the osteopathic principles.

question: Give the glossary definition of somatic dysfunction.
cited_learning_objective: Define somatic dysfunction.
answer: Impaired or altered function of related components of the somatic (body framework) system; skeletal, arthrodial, and myofascial structures, and related vascular, lymphatic, and neural elements.
rationale: The definition includes the musculoskeletal framework and the vascular, lymphatic, and neural elements related to it.

question: The acronym TART, used to identify somatic dysfunction, stands for tissue texture changes, __________, restricted motion, and tenderness.
cited_learning_objective: Expand the A in TART.
answer: asymmetry
rationale: TART is tissue texture changes, asymmetry, restricted motion, and tenderness.

question: AROM stands for __________ range of motion. PROM stands for __________ range of motion. __________ range of motion is typically greater than __________ range of motion.
cited_learning_objective: Expand AROM and PROM and state which is typically greater.
answer: active, passive, passive, active
rationale: AROM is active range of motion and PROM is passive range of motion. PROM is typically greater than AROM.
accept: active range of motion, passive range of motion, passive, active

question: __________ range of motion is reduced when a patient does not extend with maximal effort. __________ range of motion is reduced when a patient does not fully relax the agonist and antagonist muscles.
cited_learning_objective: State which range of motion falls with poor effort and which falls with incomplete relaxation.
answer: active, passive
rationale: AROM falls when effort is incomplete. PROM falls when the patient does not fully relax.
accept: active range of motion, passive range of motion

question: Somatic dysfunction is treatable using __________.
cited_learning_objective: Name the treatment used for somatic dysfunction.
answer: osteopathic manipulative treatment
rationale: Somatic dysfunction is treatable with osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT).

question: The indication for osteopathic manipulative treatment is __________.
cited_learning_objective: Name the indication for OMT.
answer: somatic dysfunction
rationale: Somatic dysfunction is the indication for OMT.

question: Name the end-feel for each passive motion. Elbow extension: __________. Knee flexion: __________. Ankle dorsiflexion: __________.
cited_learning_objective: Match end-feel to elbow extension, knee flexion, and ankle dorsiflexion.
answer: bony or hard, soft tissue approximation, soft tissue stretch
rationale: Elbow extension is bony or hard. Knee flexion is soft tissue approximation. Ankle dorsiflexion is soft tissue stretch.
accept: hard, soft tissue approximation, soft tissue stretch
bone, soft tissue approximation, soft tissue stretch

question: Match each scenario to the osteopathic tenet or tenets it best illustrates. A scenario may match more than one. Tenets: A the body is a unit; B the body is self-regulating and self-healing; C structure and function are reciprocally related; D rational treatment is based on applying these principles. Scenarios: (1) Jaw joint pain improves with a heel lift on the side of a shorter leg. (2) Low back pain improves after the patient transfers away from a disliked supervisor. (3) Mid-thoracic tenderness and asymmetric motion share nerve supply with an inflamed stomach. (4) High stress increases the frequency of upper respiratory infections.
cited_learning_objective: Apply the osteopathic tenets to four clinical scenarios.
answer: 1 maps to A and C. 2 maps to A and B. 3 maps to A and C. 4 maps to A. Each scenario illustrates that the body is a unit. The heel lift and the visceral-somatic example also show that structure and function are reciprocally related. The job change illustrates self-regulation once an impediment is removed.
rationale: The packet keys more than one tenet for some scenarios, so this item is written rather than a single-answer match.

question: Describe the difference between osteopathic manipulative medicine (OMM) and osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT).
cited_learning_objective: Distinguish OMM from OMT.
answer: OMM is the broader application of osteopathic philosophy, principles, and practices in diagnosis and management. It includes history, examination, data gathering, and treatment, and it typically includes a structural exam and OMT, though OMT is not required for the term. OMT is specifically the hands-on manipulative techniques used to treat somatic dysfunction.
rationale: Keep OMM as the whole process and OMT as the hands-on technique.

question: Describe the distinction between osteopathic manipulative medicine (OMM) and osteopathic principles and practices (OPP).
cited_learning_objective: Distinguish OMM from OPP.
answer: OMM is the application of osteopathic philosophy, principles, and practices in diagnosing and managing a patient, typically including the structural examination and OMT. OPP is the collection of philosophical principles, tenets, explanatory models, examination procedures, patient-management techniques, and manual techniques associated with osteopathic physicians. OMM is distinct from other medical practice because it incorporates OPP.
rationale: OPP is the body of principles and methods. OMM is their application in care.

question: Which is typically greater, active range of motion or passive range of motion, and why?
cited_learning_objective: Compare AROM and PROM.
answer: Passive range of motion is typically greater than active range of motion. Active motion is reduced when the patient does not use maximal effort. Passive motion is reduced when the patient does not fully relax the agonist and antagonist muscles.
rationale: State that passive motion is typically greater, then give both reasons.

question: List the five commonly discussed models of osteopathic evaluation and treatment.
cited_learning_objective: Name the five osteopathic models.
answer: Biomechanical, respiratory-circulatory, neurologic, metabolic-energy, and behavioral.
rationale: Name all five.

question: Provide one clinical example of how each of the five osteopathic models can guide treatment.
cited_learning_objective: Give a treatment example for each osteopathic model.
answer: Biomechanical: muscle energy for sacroiliac dysfunction. Respiratory-circulatory: thoracic inlet release to enhance lymphatic return. Neurologic: suboccipital release to reduce sympathetic overactivity. Metabolic-energy: lymphatic pump techniques to support immune response. Behavioral: counseling on stress reduction and sleep hygiene.
rationale: One example for each model is enough.

question: Describe the difference between type I and type II somatic dysfunction according to Fryette's principles.
cited_learning_objective: Contrast type I and type II Fryette mechanics.
answer: Type I dysfunction occurs when the spine is neutral. Sidebending and rotation occur in opposite directions and typically involve multiple vertebrae. Type II dysfunction occurs when the spine is flexed or extended. Sidebending and rotation occur to the same side and usually involve a single segment.
rationale: Include neutral versus flexed or extended, the coupling direction, and group versus single segment.

question: How does the principle that structure and function are reciprocally related influence diagnosis and treatment planning?
cited_learning_objective: Apply the structure-function principle to a plan.
answer: The clinician assesses both structural alignment or restriction and the physiology that dysfunction affects. Rib restriction, for example, may impair lymph flow or breathing. Treatment considers how restoring structure with OMT can support circulation or nerve activity.
rationale: Pair a structural finding with a functional consequence.

question: Describe a real or hypothetical case in which self-regulation or self-healing explains a patient's improvement. How would that change the counseling?
cited_learning_objective: Apply self-regulation to patient counseling.
answer: Ankle swelling that improves with rest and elevation, without another intervention, demonstrates self-regulation. Counseling explains that the body has mechanisms to restore balance, and that the physician's role is to remove barriers through OMT, movement, or lifestyle change so those processes can work.
rationale: Name a recovery and the counseling that follows from it.

question: When performing a structural exam, how might observation of posture guide palpatory findings and hypotheses?
cited_learning_objective: Connect posture observation to palpation.
answer: If one shoulder is higher, expect increased tone in the upper trapezius or decreased tone in latissimus dorsi on that side, and look for somatic dysfunction influencing those muscles. Posture directs palpation and helps the findings fit together.
rationale: Start from one visible asymmetry and predict the tissues you will palpate.

question: How can understanding anatomic planes and axes improve the precision and safety of OMT?
cited_learning_objective: Relate planes and axes to safe technique.
answer: Knowing the plane and axis of a motion helps position the patient and direct force toward or away from a barrier. It also keeps the force inside the joint's normal biomechanics, which reduces strain.
rationale: Tie the plane and axis to both accuracy and safety.

question: Why are somatic dysfunctions named for their position of ease rather than their restriction? What does this convention reveal about the osteopathic approach?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the ease-of-motion naming convention.
answer: Naming for the position of ease is an agreed convention. It removes ambiguity and lets practitioners communicate a dysfunction concisely and clearly.
rationale: The packet's model answer emphasizes clear communication, not a claim that ease is more important than the barrier.

question: How do the five models of osteopathic care support a more complete understanding of the patient beyond the immediate musculoskeletal findings?
cited_learning_objective: Use the five models to widen the assessment.
answer: The models ask the clinician to consider circulation, neurology, metabolism, and behavior along with structure. The plan can then address the whole person rather than one musculoskeletal finding.
rationale: Show that the models add systems beyond the local somatic finding.

question: Compare a strictly biomedical explanation of low back pain with an osteopathic interpretation. What additional insights does the osteopathic framework provide?
cited_learning_objective: Contrast biomedical and osteopathic views of low back pain.
answer: A biomedical view might focus on a herniated disc compressing a nerve. An osteopathic approach also considers compensatory posture, diaphragm motion, emotional stress, and autonomic imbalance, which can contribute to the problem and widen the treatment options.
rationale: Keep the disc example, then add the osteopathic factors.

question: A patient has chronic neck tension and stress. How could you apply both the behavioral and neurologic models?
cited_learning_objective: Apply the behavioral and neurologic models to neck tension.
answer: The behavioral model leads to discussion of sleep, stress reduction, and breathing. The neurologic model guides OMT such as suboccipital release to decrease sympathetic tone. Together they address physical and emotional contributors.
rationale: Give one behavioral step and one neurologic technique.

question: In what ways can palpation serve as both a diagnostic and a therapeutic tool?
cited_learning_objective: Describe diagnostic and therapeutic palpation.
answer: Palpation identifies tissue texture change and tenderness. The same careful touch can calm, reduce muscle tension, support relaxation, and build a therapeutic relationship.
rationale: Separate what palpation finds from what the touch itself can do.

question: How does the osteopathic emphasis on structure, function, and the whole person prepare you to collaborate with other healthcare professionals?
cited_learning_objective: Connect whole-person reasoning to interprofessional care.
answer: The clinician sees a condition as involving more than one system and can explain how musculoskeletal findings relate to medical, surgical, or psychological factors. That supports teamwork and lets osteopathic care sit alongside other approaches.
rationale: Show how a structural finding is communicated to another profession.

question: Flexion and extension occur in the __________ plane about a __________ axis.
cited_learning_objective: State the plane and axis of flexion and extension.
answer: sagittal, transverse
rationale: Flexion and extension occur in the sagittal plane about a transverse (left-right) axis.

question: Sidebending occurs in the __________ plane about an __________ axis.
cited_learning_objective: State the plane and axis of sidebending.
answer: coronal, anterior-posterior
rationale: Sidebending occurs in the coronal plane about an anterior-posterior axis.

question: Rotation occurs in the __________ plane about a __________ axis.
cited_learning_objective: State the plane and axis of rotation.
answer: transverse, superior-inferior
rationale: Rotation occurs in the transverse plane about a superior-inferior (vertical) axis.

question: On a diagram of joint motion, the inner pair of normal barriers, inside which active motion usually occurs, are the normal __________ barriers.
cited_learning_objective: Name the inner barriers on a joint-motion diagram.
answer: physiologic
rationale: The inner pair are the normal physiologic barriers. A restrictive barrier may or may not lie inside them.

question: On a diagram of joint motion, the outer pair of barriers that mark the limit of passive motion are the __________ barriers.
cited_learning_objective: Name the outer barriers on a joint-motion diagram.
answer: anatomic
rationale: The outer pair are the anatomic barriers. A restrictive barrier always lies within them.

question: The barrier that shifts the midline away from itself and causes loss of motion in one direction is the __________ barrier.
cited_learning_objective: Name the barrier that shifts neutral and limits motion in one direction.
answer: restrictive
rationale: The restrictive barrier shifts the usual midline away from itself and produces loss of motion in that direction. It always lies within the anatomic barriers.
